indication: Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction
benchmarkContext: The separate JAMA Cardiology severe-HF post-hoc analysis estimates a subgroup signal but does not establish prospectively controlled replication or mortality benefit; FDA previously questioned the original NDA efficacy proof.
observedResult: Prior GALACTIC-HF Phase 3 randomized ~8232 analyzed adults with HFrEF; primary CV death or first HF event was 37.0% omecamtiv vs 39.1% placebo, HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.86–0.99), p=0.03. Cardiovascular death alone HR 1.01 (95% CI 0.92–1.11), no clear mortality improvement. Severe-HF post-hoc subgroup 510/1106 vs 611/1152, HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.71–0.90). COMET-HF is a DIFFERENT confirmatory trial with no current readout.
uncertaintyReview: The overall benefit was modest and a severe subgroup was post hoc. Different LVEF/NYHA event eligibility and care standards in COMET-HF may not reproduce the subgroup result.
criticalRiskReview: The historically small primary composite reduction and absent CV-death benefit cannot be assumed to predict the confirmatory trial's efficacy.

indication: Heart Failure With Reduced Ejection Fraction
benchmarkContext: Duke Clinical Research Institute independently describes protocol, clinical event endpoints and intended population, not a completed COMET-HF statistical review or power verification.
observedResult: COMET-HF is a new recruiting randomized, double-blind placebo-controlled Phase 3 trial of omecamtiv mecarbil in symptomatic severely reduced EF heart failure, planned ~1,800 patients. Its primary composite includes cardiovascular death, first HF event, LVAD, transplant and stroke, with event-driven ~850 planned first HF events/CV deaths; an interim futility/efficacy analysis is planned near 570 events.
uncertaintyReview: Event-driven projected 2027 study completion is NOT a company-verified exact topline announcement. SAP, event adjudication, enrollment pace and multiplicity have not been independently audited.
criticalRiskReview: Changes in composite events from GALACTIC-HF and a planned interim look may influence type-I error/power; prior CRL underscores importance of substantial evidence.

benchmarkContext: FDA's historical REXULTI schizophrenia trial snapshot demonstrates six-week PANSS as an accepted clinical measure, with active vs placebo differences from a separate drug and study. Not a head-to-head comparison or proof of LB-102 superiority.
observedResult: Prior NOVA-1 Phase 2 schizophrenia RCT NCT06179108 randomized 359 adults. At Week 4 PANSS total change was -14.3 with 50 mg, -14.0 with 75 mg, and -9.3 placebo; placebo-subtracted 50 mg difference -5.0 (95% CI -8.0 to -2.1; p<0.001) and 75 mg difference -4.7 (95% CI -7.7 to -1.7; p=0.002), Hochberg-adjusted. No Phase 3 NOVA-2 efficacy is known.
uncertaintyReview: Four-week Phase 2 was predominantly inpatient with 81.6% 4-week completion. Phase 3 evaluates 50 mg and 100 mg at Week 6; the 100 mg prior group was only n=36, and its p value was nominal, not in the original pairwise primary multiple-testing family.
criticalRiskReview: Limited 100 mg prior dose evidence, attrition and high laboratory prolactin/weight change may undermine replicated Phase 3 benefit-risk despite statistically positive Phase 2.

benchmarkContext: NOVA-3 registry specifies long-term safety and tolerability, whereas prior NOVA-1 reports acute-inpatient 4-week efficacy. The populations, endpoints and contrast designs differ.
observedResult: Prior placebo-controlled NOVA-1 Phase 2 in acute schizophrenia (NCT06179108) had Week-4 PANSS improvement: 50 mg LB-102 -14.3 versus placebo -9.3, difference -5.0 (95% CI -8.0 to -2.1). NOVA-3 is a distinct 52-week OPEN-LABEL SAFETY study in stable schizophrenia; it is NOT a second blinded efficacy replication.
uncertaintyReview: NOVA-1 acute efficacy may not transfer to chronic stable patients switched from other antipsychotics; no placebo counterfactual in NOVA-3; attrition over one year unknown.
criticalRiskReview: Do not score long-term NOVA-3 efficacy as if a randomized Phase 3 PANSS advantage has been shown or as the NOVA-2 pivotal efficacy readout.

benchmarkContext: The exact registry NCT identifies a long-duration safety study and distinguishes it from randomized 6-week pivotal NOVA-2. Open-label design can contribute exposure and tolerability but not controlled efficacy proof.
observedResult: Issuer describes NOVA-3 as a 52-week OPEN-LABEL study evaluating long-term safety and tolerability of LB-102 in stable schizophrenia, accepting patients transitioning from NOVA-2 and other participants. No randomized concurrent placebo arm is planned for this safety cohort.
uncertaintyReview: Open-label selection, unblinded tolerability, prior drug exposure and inadequate comparison power limit causal efficacy claims. Exact minimum exposure count and attrition handling need external verification.
criticalRiskReview: Improperly treating NOVA-3 as a placebo-controlled efficacy trial would double-count LB-102 benefit and inflate PDUFA success assumptions.

benchmarkContext: The registered 52-week NOVA-3 long-term safety plan directly addresses earlier short-term endocrine/metabolic monitoring limitations. Baseline event rates are prior study arm-level observations, not 2026 Phase 3 harms.
observedResult: Earlier NOVA-1 randomized Phase 2 found prolactin elevations in roughly 87.5-94% on LB-102 doses versus 5.2% placebo and mean weight gain from 2.9 to 4.3 kg versus 2.0 kg placebo over four weeks. NOVA-3 is designed to collect up to 52 weeks of safety, but these results do not yet exist.
uncertaintyReview: NOVA-1 included a small higher-dose group and a short four-week period; clinical prolactin symptoms, 1-year metabolic/sexual effects and withdrawals under NOVA-3 remain unknown.
criticalRiskReview: Long-term endocrine/metabolic burden and open-label safety ascertainment may materially alter risk-benefit; no independent external safety signoff.

benchmarkContext: FDA final guidance on multiplicity motivates evaluating prespecified families and dose comparisons. Matched CORAL randomized placebo controls and reported CIs provide within-trial evidence; guidance does not set an independent clinically meaningful cough reduction threshold.
observedResult: The prior CORAL Phase 2b IPF cough trial NCT05964335 randomized 165 patients (160 in primary analysis): six-week objectively measured 24-hour cough count fell 60.2% with nalbuphine ER 108 mg twice daily versus 16.9% placebo; log scale placebo difference -1.03 (95% CI -1.48 to -0.58), p<0.001. The 27 and 54 mg doses also met reported cough count comparisons. This is not an OCEAN-1 result.
uncertaintyReview: Prior Phase 2b with 160 analyzed, three dose arms, and protocol sensitivity questions; the 52-week OCEAN-1 primary estimand and longer-term treatment effect have not been observed. Objective cough reduction does not itself establish survival or functional benefit.
criticalRiskReview: High dose had marked nausea/tolerability concerns, previous six-week effects may not persist for 52 weeks. Do not double-count OCEAN-2 or earlier Phase 2b as completed OCEAN-1 efficacy.

benchmarkContext: The peer-reviewed preceding CORAL RCT used objective 24-hour cough frequency at six weeks. OCEAN-1 evaluates a much longer schedule, making dose, durability, missing data and patient-rated outcomes key translational questions.
observedResult: Trevi said first pivotal IPF-related cough OCEAN-1 trial began Q2 2026 and has 52-week fixed dosing; Phase 3 research NCT07671911 is recruiting. This design follows a randomized placebo-controlled phase 2b CORAL trial showing a signal in objective cough count.
uncertaintyReview: Full OCEAN-1 SAP/power assumptions and multiplicity hierarchy are not independently adjudicated in the current source. Trial recruitment and design cannot establish an eventual positive Phase 3 readout.
criticalRiskReview: Long follow-up increases attrition and compliance uncertainty. The second pivotal OCEAN-2 must not be mistaken for the same 52-week study.

benchmarkContext: FDA clinical development framework requires a full benefit-risk assessment and long-term safety; safety figures are comparisons within the preceding controlled Phase 2b trial, not independent active-agent comparators.
observedResult: Prior CORAL Phase 2b placebo-controlled safety: pooled nalbuphine ER serious AEs 1.6% versus 10.0% placebo, but nausea 33.6% versus 5.0%, vomiting 21.0% versus 0%, constipation 20.0% versus 0%. Any AE-driven study-drug discontinuation 5.6% active vs 5.0% placebo. Dose 108 mg had 50.0% nausea. No current OCEAN-1 Phase 3 safety outcome is available.
uncertaintyReview: CORAL treatment was six weeks, whereas OCEAN-1 follows up to 52 weeks. Small sample size, differential gastrointestinal adverse events, and unresolved chronic-use safety limit extrapolation; no independent long-term study safety signoff.
criticalRiskReview: High rates of nausea, vomiting and dizziness at dose; 52-week discontinuation and serious toxicity cannot be predicted from the 6-week CORAL population.

benchmarkContext: The source registry identifies the prospective OCEAN-2 program distinct from prior controlled CORAL; the benchmark is earlier randomized cough-frequency benefit, not an independent drug-versus-standard-treatment safety comparison.

OCEAN-2 is the separate 14-week Phase 3 study and has no efficacy readout.
uncertaintyReview: A 6-week CORAL signal is not proof of 14-week Phase 3 success, durable function or clinically relevant reduction after dose changes; the three dose arms and familywise testing require independent review.
criticalRiskReview: Uncertain maintenance of effect, dosing consistency, and gastrointestinal adverse events after 14 weeks. Do not borrow OCEAN-1 timing or Phase 3 results.

benchmarkContext: The registered OCEAN-2 Phase 3 trial extends controlled exposure to 14 weeks, so prior short-duration tolerability must be stressed rather than asserted to generalize.

criticalRiskReview: Potential dose-limiting gastrointestinal intolerance, dropout and unreported longer-term harms could overwhelm a positive cough reduction effect.
